text:
A 2026 review brought together 26 studies involving more than 2,000 adults to ask a focused question. What happens when safety behaviours are targeted on their own, outside formal exposure work? Safety behaviours are the things people do to prevent anxiety or a feared outcome, such as mirror checking, avoiding eye contact or searching symptoms online. Across the studies, cutting back on these behaviours was linked with fewer symptoms than control conditions, and in experiments with students, being asked to increase them was linked with more. The authors describe this as grounds for cautious optimism.

Why this matters across roles: most of the included studies did not involve a clinician, and many used simple daily reminders sent by phone or online. These behaviours show up in everyday moments, so people in many roles are well placed to notice them.

One practical takeaway: notice the small things a person does to feel safe, and get curious rather than correcting. A gentle question such as "What do you worry might happen if you did not do that?" can open a useful conversation. If these habits seem to keep fear going, talk with the person about involving their GP or a psychologist.

Where the evidence stops:
• Most participants were young women, many recruited through universities.
• Published results may overstate the benefit for symptoms.
• Few studies looked at OCD or PTSD, and exposure therapy itself was outside this review.

Key source: Goodson et al., 2026: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2026.102703
